questions.story:
On Fresh Air in the Sickroom
Adapted from Florence Nightingale’s "Notes on Nursing"

Passage 1:
There is no requirement in the care of the sick more important than the supply of fresh air. To keep the air a patient breathes as pure as the outside air, without chilling him, is the very first canon of nursing. Every nurse who neglects this single rule will fail her patient in every other respect as well. It is not one duty among many. It is the foundation upon which every other act of care must rest, and without it no recovery can honestly be expected.

Passage 2:
The evidence on this point is considerable. Returns collected from twelve London hospitals between 1854 and 1857 show that wards with continuous window ventilation recorded a mortality rate of nine per cent, compared with twenty-two per cent in wards where windows remained closed. The Army Sanitary Commission reported a similar pattern in 1858, finding that barracks with improved ventilation saw fever cases fall by more than half within a single year. These are not impressions gathered at the bedside. They are counted results, taken across many hundreds of patients.

Passage 3:
Many experienced nurses will also tell you that they can sense at once, on entering a room, whether the air within it is wholesome, and this feeling is widely shared throughout the profession. Families, too, frequently observe that a patient appears easier after a window has been opened. It may be added that St Thomas’s Hospital was first established in the twelfth century and has been rebuilt on three separate occasions since. Its present buildings are much admired for their handsome brickwork and the fine proportions of their long corridors.

Passage 4:
Against all this stands the ruinous, suffocating superstition that night air is dangerous. What appalling nonsense this is, and what untold harm it has done. Timid attendants seal their windows at dusk and leave the sick to breathe the same foul, exhausted air until morning, poisoning by slow degrees the very patients they imagine themselves to be protecting. A nurse who does this is not merely failing in her duty; she is actively working against the recovery of the person in her charge. No good whatever has ever come of a closed window.

Passage 5:
Naturally, every intelligent person now accepts that fresh air is essential to the sick. The only question remaining is how quickly hospitals and households will act upon what they already plainly know. Let the windows be opened, and let every objection be set aside without further discussion. In a single generation the health of the nation might be transformed entirely. Those who still hesitate at so simple a measure have evidently not considered the matter with the seriousness it deserves, for the case is, and has always been, perfectly plain.

questions.story:
Ozymandias
By Percy Bysshe Shelley

I met a traveller from an antique land,
Who said—“Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert. . . . Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed;
And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away.”
